description: I am a developer with a master’s degree in Systems Engineering. I have more than five years of experience in software development, artificial intelligence, digital transformation, and technology leadership. I am currently leading THE ORIGIN PROJECT for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, an immersive educational platform based on real astronomical data from SPHEREx. I am looking for collaborators who are passionate about science, technology, and innovation.
summary:
Imagine a Google Maps of the universe, but in infrared light with a built-in time machine. NASA releases terabytes of real data from its SPHEREx space telescope, yet it sits locked in complex scientific files almost no one can open.
The Origin Project transforms those multi-epoch infrared datasets into an interactive digital observatory accessible to everyone. Users can locate regions of the sky by coordinates or object names, analyze changes in brightness and motion over time, and explore faint Solar System candidates—such as Planet X—without needing specialized astrophysics software.
Additionally, the platform lets users save and export their research sessions in PDF and JSON formats so they can document and resume their analyses without losing progress. Every exported session incorporates a SHA-256 digital fingerprint calculated over its measurements, candidates, and FITS cutout hashes to ensure data integrity and verify that results remain unaltered—democratizing space exploration with scientific rigor.
details:
The concept: ‘The Origin Project’ is an interactive astronomical observatory designed to make the infrared datasets from NASA’s SPHEREx mission intuitive, quick to access and verifiable. Rather than requiring specialised astrophysics software to examine FITS files or multi-epoch catalogues, users can query the sky directly using right ascension (RA) and declination (Dec) in decimal degrees. They can also compare measurements from different epochs with published values and export discovery reports featuring tamper-proof integrity mechanisms.
Key features
• Interactive navigation of the sky map: thanks to Aladin Lite, users can pan and zoom the infrared sky image over a SPHEREx base layer covering the entire sky (spherex_allsky_cube), with a colour overlay from AllWISE (P/allWISE/colour) and layers from the Gaia DR3 catalogue.
• Navigation using sexagesimal coordinates and an astronomical ‘time machine’: Enter celestial coordinates in standard sexagesimal (or decimal) format for Right Ascension (RA) and Declination (Dec) — or identify object names via SIMBAD — to automatically centre the sky map on that region and compare how the brightness of objects varies across multiple observation epochs.
• ‘Planet X’ mode (Shift-and-Stack): Implements shift-and-stack processing to detect faint, slow-moving Solar System objects across different epochs, as demonstrated using the known cold brown dwarf WISE 0855-0714 as a reference.
• Verifiable research reports (SHA-256): Each research session calculates an SHA-256 cryptographic hash of its main content (measurements, candidates and FITS crop hashes). Reports are exported in PDF and JSON formats (with generation timestamps in UTC) and include instructions for independently recalculating the hash and verifying data integrity.
Technology stack
• Frontend: Next.js, React and Aladin Lite for interactive astronomical visualisation.
• Backend: Python with FastAPI, astroquery and scientific FITS processing for coordinate queries, multi-epoch photometry and ‘shift-and-stack’ analysis.
• Database and hosting: Supabase (PostgreSQL) for session persistence, deployed on Vercel and Railway.
